The donor sign identifies a ‘circa 1820 Greek Revival building’ donated by Mr. and Mrs. C. Franklin Bendall. UAH Archives separately catalogs an item titled ‘1835 Union Chapel Church, Hazel Green, 1972’ in the Harvie P. Jones papers, Box 73, Folder 9; the catalog page does not identify a denomination or African American congregation.
Why It Is Important: Documents the 1973–1975 relocation and museum conversion, names Harvie Jones as preservation advocate, and preserves conflicting descriptions of the building’s date, denomination, and identity. The official catalog’s silence does not prove erasure, and this evidence does not prove a Black congregation, a Jones-family relationship, or a plantation-network connection.

Document Title: Virgil Carrington Jones, “Quietdale” (1992; text dated 1969)
Document Type: Secondary local-history and architectural article incorporating attributed recollection
Source: Virgil Carrington Jones; The Historic Huntsville Quarterly, vol. 18, no. 3, article 15; UAH LOUIS

Document Title: Alabama's 1865, 1875, and 1901 Constitutions — the 'punishment for crime' slavery exception, in force almost word-for-word from 1865 until Alabama voters removed it in 2022
Document Type: Primary source (state constitutional text) with secondary legal-historical synthesis
Source: Alabama Department of Archives and History digital constitutions collection; Alabama Constitution of 1901, Art. I §32

I §33: same idea, 'no involuntary servitude, otherwise than for the punishment of crime, of which the party shall have been duly convicted.' 1901, Art. I §32: nearly identical language, and this is the version that stayed on the books until the November 2022 referendum.

Conclusions: Alabama had seven constitutions total (1819, 1861, 1865, 1868, 1875, 1901, and the 2022 recompilation). Only three carried the punishment-for-crime exception forward in this form — 1865, 1875, 1901 — which is why those are the three logged here, not all seven. I haven't checked the 1868 constitution's exact wording yet, so I'm leaving that as an open thread rather than ruling it out.

Document Title: 1719 Will of Orlando Jones (proved York Co., VA) -- earliest documented enslaved individuals in the direct Avalon Jones lineage
Document Type: Original will, primary source (bequest of named enslaved people)
Source: York County, VA Court Records, Book 15 -- Deeds, Orders, Wills, p. 517, dated June 4, 1719, proved Nov. 16, 1719; published in William & Mary College Quarterly Historical Magazine, vol. 8; reproduced in Harrison & Cape family history, Chapter 4 ("Scholarship-Articles_Harrison-Cape-Manuscript-Chapter-4-Macon_undated_[4-Macon].pdf")
Evidence: Orlando Jones's will names at least 20 enslaved individuals in three bequests: (1) to wife Mary Jones -- Frank, "a molatto woman Slave... with all her increase"; (2) to son LANE JONES (direct Avalon-line ancestor) -- Hannah, Ned, David, Sarah, Selton, Jenney ("great Jenney"), Warwick, Jemmy, and Old Jack ("at Cohoke"); (3) to daughter Frances Jones (who married Col. John Dandridge and became grandmother of Martha Washington -- a collateral, non-Avalon branch) -- Nanny ("Cohoke"), Jemmy, Gabriel, Poll, Johnny, Dinah, Kate, Kate's unnamed "Girl Jenney," Dick, and John Ried (also transcribed "John Bird" in the family-history copy). The will separately gives "my Servant Will Kanadey" to Lane Jones -- described as a servant, not a slave.
Why It Is Important: This is the earliest documented instance in this study of the direct Avalon-lineage enslaver family (Orlando Jones -> Lane Jones -> Frances Barber Jones -> Lewellen Jones -> Madison Co., AL) explicitly holding and bequeathing enslaved people by name, roughly 80-100 years before the 1803-1824 Virginia-to-Alabama land transactions already logged in this database (rows 317-320). It shows the practice of treating enslaved people as transferable, name-tracked, generationally-reproducing property (see the 'increase' clause for Frank) was present from the family's earliest Virginia generation. Wikipedia's secondary summary states Orlando Jones "owned 21 enslaved persons" total, closely matching this study's count of 20 named individuals across the three bequests.
Connections: Direct lineage: Orlando Jones -> Lane Jones (m. Ann Barber, 1727) -> Frances Barber Jones (m. Capt. John Jones) -> Lewellen Jones (b. 1760, d. 1820) -> John Nelson Spottswood Jones -> Madison Co., AL Jones-Donnell line (DB1 rows 314-320). Collateral (non-Avalon) branch: Orlando's daughter Frances Jones m. Col. John Dandridge -> grandmother of Martha Dandridge Custis Washington.
Conclusions: The record indicates enslaved individuals were being named, divided among heirs, and tracked generationally within this family at least three generations before the 1803-1824 Virginia/Alabama land-and-labor records already logged. The nine people bequeathed to Lane Jones are the closest documented ancestors-in-bondage to the eventual Madison County, Alabama plantation line, though no direct documentary link connecting these named individuals to later Madison Co. estate records has yet been found.
Questions: No later record has yet been found tracing Hannah, Ned, David, Sarah, Selton, Jenney, Warwick, Jemmy, or Old Jack (Lane Jones's 1719 bequest) forward through subsequent generations or westward to Alabama; not established whether any of these individuals or descendants were later held by Lewellen Jones or moved to Madison Co., AL. "John Ried" vs. "John Bird" is a transcription discrepancy between two source copies needing resolution against the original York County court record. "Lucy Jones" (DB2, already logged) relationship to this Orlando Jones line remains unconfirmed. Ages and specific race designations were not recorded in the will for most individuals.

(2) Confirms with exact dates that TWO marriages tied the Jones and Anderson families together in one generation: Lewellen Jones m. Mary Louise Anderson (10-22-1792) AND, separately, Lewellen's sister Elizabeth West Jones (1778-1838) m. Jesse Anderson (1776-1818, Nelson Anderson's son) on 6-21-1791 (Marriage Bonds, Bedford Co. Va.). (3) Independently reproduces the exact citation for the 1797 John S. Jones estate appraisal already flagged as a DB4 lead: 'Appraisement of Estate of Captain John S. The double Jones-Anderson marriage (both directions, same generation) is a textbook case of elite endogamous kinship consolidation described in the sociological literature on planter-class family networks -- land, enslaved people, and social capital were kept within a tight cluster of allied families across two marriages simultaneously.

Document Type: Biographical/vital-record compilation (secondary, citing tombstone, Yale records, county marriage record, federal land patent)
Source: Harrison & Cape family history, Chapter 9.5 ("Scholarship-Articles_Harrison-Cape-Manuscript-Chapter-9.5-Clopton-Part-2-and-John-Nelson-Spotswood_undated_[9.5-Clopton Part 2 and John Nelson Spotswood].pdf"), citing tombstone inscription at "Druid's Grove," Greenbrier, Limestone Co., Ala.; Yale University Library correspondence, Nov. 1967; Davidson County, TN First Marriage Book p. 244; U.S. Bureau of Land Management Certificate No. 820, Vol. 109, pp. 124/137
Evidence: John Nelson Spottswood Jones, eldest son of Capt. Lewellen Jones and Mary Louisa Anderson, born Sept. 1, 1793, Louisa Co., VA; emigrated c. 1805 to Mississippi Territory with his parents and brother Alexander Pinckney Jones; received an 1813 Madison Co., AL land patent (Cert. No. 820, SW1/4 Sec. 10, Twp. 2, Range 1 West, 157.75 acres); graduated Yale, Class of 1819; read law under Judge John Haywood at "Tusculum," Nashville; opened a Huntsville law office in 1819 and helped found the Huntsville Library (first in Alabama, incorporated Nov. 27, 1819); married Eliza Ann Haywood, daughter of Judge John Haywood, March 5, 1821, at "Tusculum"; the couple settled at "Druid's Grove," Greenbrier, Limestone Co., AL, where twelve children were born; Eliza Ann died Sept. 17, 1852; John N.S. Jones died Nov. 17, 1853.
Why It Is Important: Directly connects the Jones/Avalon family to Judge John Haywood (subject of the next chapter in this sweep, ch. 10) via a marriage one generation before the Avalon-era Jones descendants, and situates the family within Huntsville's earliest civic/professional institutions (law practice, public library), evidencing the social capital that accompanied their landed and enslaved-labor wealth.
Connections: Capt. Lewellen Jones & Mary Louisa Anderson (parents); Judge John Haywood (father-in-law, ch. 10 subject); Alexander Pinckney Jones (brother, see companion row above); sisters Harriett (m. Dr. David Moore of Huntsville) and Martha (m. Col. Branch Jones of Tuscumbia, AL); sister Frances Anna Mariah Jones (m. Benjamin Perkins, remained in VA).
Conclusions: The record indicates a consistent multi-generational strategy of consolidating land, enslaved labor, and elite marriage alliances, paralleling the Clopton/Anderson patterns already documented in chapter 9 (DB1 row 325).
Questions: No enslaved individuals are named in this biographical material. The enslaved population of "Druid's Grove" plantation is not yet documented -- a research gap to revisit during the DB5 plantations-network phase.
Citation: Yale University Library archives; Davidson County, TN marriage records; U.S. BLM Eastern States Land Office patent records; family-history transcription in Harrison & Cape, Captain Llewellen Jones, ch. 9.5 ("Scholarship-Articles_Harrison-Cape-Manuscript-Chapter-9.5-Clopton-Part-2-and-John-Nelson-Spotswood_undated_[9.5-Clopton Part 2 and John Nelson Spotswood].pdf")

VA; emigrated c.1805 to Mississippi Territory; 1813 Madison Co. land patent; Yale graduate, Huntsville Library founder; m. Eliza Ann Haywood (daughter of Judge John Haywood)

Document Title: John Haywood Jones (1826-1866) -- major Limestone Co. planter; Ragland/Bird/Gordon/Druid's Grove tracts; postwar ruin
Document Type: Newspaper feature (secondary/local history), as reproduced in family-history transcription
Source: "Limestone's Historic Homes -- From First, The Westmoreland Home Embodied South's Flavor Of Romance," newspaper article, reproduced in Harrison & Cape family history, Chapter 10 ("Scholarship-Articles_Harrison-Cape-Manuscript-Chapter-10-Haywood_undated_[10-Haywood].pdf")
Evidence: John Haywood Jones, eldest son of J.N.S. Jones and Eliza Ann Haywood, married Sallie Maria Collier (niece of Alabama Governor Henry W. Collier) Dec. 6, 1848. Held the 1,180-acre 'Ragland' tract, 700-acre 'Bird' tract, and 400-acre 'Gordon' tract (all Limestone Co., AL), plus his father's inherited 500-acre 'Druid's Grove' plantation. Built a prewar home ('Westmoreland'/'Coman Hall') in Athens, AL with bricks made on-site by enslaved people. Two children: William Haywood Jones and Alexander Spottswood Jones. Lost his home, enslaved workforce, and fortune after the Civil War; a failed postwar cotton investment left him destitute; died Aug. 13, 1866, age 40, at Druid's Grove.
Why It Is Important: Documents the scale of land and enslaved-labor wealth accumulated by the second generation of the Jones-Haywood marriage, and its abrupt reversal at emancipation and after -- direct evidence for the paper's land/capital-in-today's-dollars analysis and for DB5 (Plantations Network).
Connections: Feeds DB5 inputs (Ragland, Bird, Gordon, Druid's Grove tracts). Son of J.N.S. Jones and Eliza Ann Haywood (DB1 row 327); brother-in-law of James W.S. Donnell (m. Maria Louisa Jones) and William A. Adair (m. Octavia Isabella Jones); married into the Collier family (niece of Gov. Henry W. Collier).
Conclusions: A textbook case of planter-class wealth built on enslaved labor and land concentration collapsing at emancipation -- consistent with the broader sociological pattern of postwar downward mobility documented among large slaveholding families in Reconstruction-era Southern historiography.
Questions: Exact acreage/location of the enslaved-made brick house and the number of people enslaved at each tract are not given in this newspaper account. No enslaved individuals are named in this source.
Citation: "Limestone's Historic Homes...," reproduced in Harrison & Cape, Captain Llewellen Jones, ch. 10 ("Scholarship-Articles_Harrison-Cape-Manuscript-Chapter-10-Haywood_undated_[10-Haywood].pdf")

Document Title: "Uncle Isaac" -- formerly enslaved coachman for the Jones family; documented in 1876 as independently running a former plantation of his own
Document Type: Newspaper reminiscence column (near-contemporary secondary source, 1876), as reproduced in family-history transcription
Source: "Old Times About Athens" (serialized column, continued from prior week), The Athens Post, Athens, AL, Aug. 4, 1876; reproduced in Harrison & Cape family history, Chapter 10 ("Scholarship-Articles_Harrison-Cape-Manuscript-Chapter-10-Haywood_undated_[10-Haywood].pdf")
Evidence: An 1876 newspaper reminiscence names 'Uncle Isaac' as the enslaved coachman who, before the Civil War, drove the Jones daughters ('young missuses') to town in 'his four in hand of milk-white steeds.' The same column reports that, by 1876, Isaac 'is running a big plantation once the property of his old marster.' The passage identifies 'Mrs. Donnell's father, Mr. Jones' -- confirmed via the same chapter's Family Bible to be John Nelson Spottswood Jones, whose daughter Maria Louisa Jones married Major James W.S. Donnell.
Why It Is Important: A rare, near-contemporary (only ~11 years after emancipation) documented example of a formerly enslaved individual from the Jones/Druid's Grove plantation achieving independent economic agency on land once belonging to his enslaver -- directly supporting this project's standing priority of tracing post-emancipation Black economic continuity and preserving the humanity and agency of enslaved and formerly enslaved people rather than reducing them to property records alone.
Connections: Enslaved at 'Druid's Grove,' Limestone Co., AL, by John Nelson Spottswood Jones (DB1 row 327); connects to the Donnell family (Maria Louisa Jones m. James W.S. Donnell) referenced in the same column; relevant to upcoming William Donnell/Robert Donnell chapters (12, 14).
Conclusions: This account should be read critically: it is filtered through a white newspaper columnist's nostalgic, paternalistic voice ('his old marster'), which requires reading against the grain to recover Isaac's own agency and achievement.
Questions: Isaac's surname, the size/location of the plantation he ran by 1876, and any post-1876 record of him (census, land records, etc.) are not yet identified. Whether he purchased, rented, or sharecropped the land is not specified.
Citation: "Old Times About Athens," The Athens Post, Aug. 4, 1876, reproduced in Harrison & Cape, Captain Llewellen Jones, ch. 10 ("Scholarship-Articles_Harrison-Cape-Manuscript-Chapter-10-Haywood_undated_[10-Haywood].pdf")

Notes: 1876 newspaper column; the 'his old marster' framing requires critical reading

Document Title: 1866 Chancery Court settlement of Alexander Pinckney Jones's estate -- confirms his actual death year as 1866, not 1857
Document Type: Court record (Chancery Court, as reproduced in family-history transcription)
Source: "Alexander P. Jones, dec'd, Application to Sell Lands," Madison County Chancery Court Record Book C, p. 329, filed July 28, 1866; reproduced in Harrison & Cape family history, Chapter 11 ("Scholarship-Articles_Harrison-Cape-Manuscript-Chapter-11-Paul-Lewellen_undated_[11-Paul Lewellen].pdf")
Evidence: Paul L. Jones, as Administrator, petitioned to sell Huntsville town lots 41 and 42 (Fountain Row) to pay debts of the estate of his uncle, Alexander P. (Pinckney) Jones, deceased. The petition names Alexander P. Jones's heirs as his nephews and nieces -- the children of his late brother J.N.S. Jones: J. Haywood Jones, Maria Donnell (w/ James W.S. Donnell), Walter B. Jones, Antonina Hansell (w/ William Hansell), Alexander S. Perkins, plus grandnephews/nieces Fannie and Spotswood Harris (minors, children of Elizabeth Jones Perkins and John R. Harris), John Y. Mills and wife Octavia Mills, and Alfred and Marcelle Dearing. The document explicitly states J. Haywood Jones and Alexander S. Perkins, 'nephews of Alexander P. Jones,' both died in 1866, prior to settlement.
Why It Is Important: This is the single strongest piece of evidence yet for the row-322/row-190 website correction: it directly documents that the actual Alexander Pinckney Jones (Avalon's historical owner, J.N.S. Jones's brother) was alive until at least 1866, dying without children of his own -- meaning ANY 1857-dated record attributed to 'Alexander P. Jones, deceased' cannot be this man, and almost certainly refers instead to his same-initialed nephew Alexander T. Jones (d. 1857). This upgrades the row-322 correction from a probable inference to a well-documented near-certainty.
Connections: Resolves the identity question first raised at row 326 and the 1857 timeline entry on the website. Names John Haywood Jones (row 333's subject in ch.10) and Alexander S. Perkins as having also died in 1866, the same year as their uncle -- suggesting a family cluster of deaths, possibly disease-related, worth further investigation. Ties into the Donnell, Hansell, Perkins, Harris, Mills, and Dearing family lines, several of which recur in upcoming chapters.
Conclusions: Because Alexander Pinckney Jones died without recorded children, his estate passed collaterally to his siblings' children -- a textbook illustration of how planter-class land and capital consolidated and then dispersed across an extended kin network rather than a single nuclear-family line, reinforcing the paper's cluster-based genealogical method.
Questions: The cause of the 1866 deaths (Alexander P. Jones, J. Haywood Jones, Alexander S. Perkins, all in the same year) is not stated -- possible epidemic or postwar hardship worth checking against Limestone/Madison County death or health records. The original Chancery Court Record Book C has not been examined directly.
Citation: "Alexander P. Jones, dec'd, Application to Sell Lands," Madison County Chancery Court Record Book C, p. 329 (1866), reproduced in Harrison & Cape, Captain Llewellen Jones, ch. 11 ("Scholarship-Articles_Harrison-Cape-Manuscript-Chapter-11-Paul-Lewellen_undated_[11-Paul Lewellen].pdf")

Document Title: Jones-Donnell Cemetery tombstones, Greenbrier, Limestone Co., AL -- grave marker confirms full name 'Alex[ander] Thomas Jones,' d. 1857, matching the disputed 1857 division record

Source: Tombstone inscriptions, Jones-Donnell Cemetery, Greenbrier, Limestone Co., AL, transcribed by family researchers; reproduced in Harrison & Cape family history, Chapter 11.5 ("Scholarship-Articles_Harrison-Cape-Manuscript-Chapter-11.5-Paul-Lewellen-Part-2_undated_[11.5-Paul Lewellen Part 2].pdf")
Evidence: A large tombstone reads: 'Alex[ander] Thomas Jones, 2nd son of J.N.S. & Eliza [A.] Jones, Born Jan. 29, 1834, Died June 3, 1857, Aged 23 years, 4 months, 4 days.' Adjacent tombstones in the same family plot include: John N.S. Jones ('Son of Lewellen and Mary Anderson,' b. Sept. 1, 1793, d. Nov. 17, 1853, 'Father of Maria Louisa Jones Donnell'); Eliza Ann Haywood ('Wife of Judge John Haywood... Daughter... Jones' (row 329) and his exact death date (June 3, 1857) and age (23) already inferred from that source. Nov. 17, 1853). Documents several additional infant/child deaths among the twelve children named in the Family Bible (row 329), consistent with that record's note that 'some died in infancy.'
Conclusions: This cluster of small tombstones for infants and young children who died between 1823 and 1853 is a stark material record of childhood mortality within even a wealthy planter family, and situates the family's wealth-building alongside significant personal loss -- useful context for the paper's discussion of the human costs bound up in this plantation network, for enslavers and enslaved people alike, without conflating the two experiences.

Document Type: Primary source (Southern Claims Commission case files, approved and barred series)
Source: U.S. Southern Claims Commission records (RG 217), Publications M1407 and M2062; NARA; Fold3.com -- https://www.fold3.com/file/763055/seaborn-jones-page-1-us-southern-claims-barred-and-disallowed-1871 ; https://www.fold3.com/file/273535645/jones-seaborn-page-1-us-southern-claims-approved-alabama-1871-1880 ; https://www.fold3.com/file/273535932/jones-seaborn-m-page-1-us-southern-claims-approved-alabama-1871-1880 ; https://www.fold3.com/file/763186/seaborn-jones-jr-page-1-us-southern-claims-barred-and-disallowed-1871
Evidence: William B. Jones, administrator of the estate of Seaborn Jones (d. intestate, Madison Co. Probate Court, April 29, 1867, estate valued under USD 3,000), filed an estate claim (No. 19875) for USD 765 in horses/mules/saddle taken by the 4th Michigan Cavalry, 1863-1865, near New Market, Madison County. The Commission found Seaborn Jones Sr. loyal but split the USD 650 award among 18 heirs, disqualifying 11 (including William B. and Morgan Jones, who served in the Confederate 4th Alabama Cavalry, and Stephen W., Thomas, John, George T., Sara, Eliza, Nancy, and Catherine Jones, who "fail to establish their loyalty"); only 7 minor heirs (Richard, Allen, Martha, Susan, Trenton, Julia, Margaret) received the USD 233.33 balance. Property witness Robert Criner, explicitly recorded as "colored," of New Market, testified alongside white witnesses. A separate, related claim for Seaborn M. Jones (No. 48063/19876) for one black mare taken at George T. Jones's mill was allowed in full (USD 100, paid 1878). In that file, Wilson Jones (Colored), age 64 (b. ~1810), formerly enslaved by George T. Jones (a distinct household from Seaborn Jones/Seaborn M. Jones), testified as a loyalty witness -- stating "we colored people thought and we still think if there was any Union men he was one" -- working as a cabinet maker and miller in New Market and signing with his mark (X). Thomas U. Green testified Seaborn Jones gave Union officers intelligence on Confederate Col. Mead's location. Seaborn Jones was arrested by Confederate cavalry in 1862, escaped, spent 1864-1867 in St. Clair County, Illinois as a carpenter.
Why It Is Important: Documents rare direct testimony from Wilson Jones (Colored), a formerly enslaved miller/cabinetmaker in New Market, Madison County, giving an explicitly Black political assessment of a white neighbor's Civil War loyalty -- and from Robert Criner (colored), a named Black witness in a white family's estate claim. Both illustrate how the Southern Claims Commission process instrumentally relied on Black testimony to validate white claimants' loyalty while providing no compensable path for the witnesses' own wartime losses. Establishes George T. Jones's mill (New Market) as a site connected to an enslaved/formerly-enslaved community distinct from the Alexander P. Jones/Avalon household, directly answering the 7.13.26 worklist item asking to "locate George T. Jones mill records and verify Wilson Jones."
Connections: George T. Jones (mill owner, enslaver of Wilson Jones); Wilson Jones (Colored); Robert Criner (colored); Seaborn Jones Sr.; William B. Jones; Seaborn M. Jones; Morgan Jones; Stephen W., Thomas, John, Sara, Eliza, Nancy, Catherine Jones (disqualified heirs); worklist item 7.13.26 #4 (Wilson Jones/George T. Jones mill)
Conclusions: The Commission's per-heir loyalty filter, which stripped 11 of 18 heirs (including named women and children given no further description) of compensation, shows institutional erasure operating even against white Unionist families through mechanical loyalty tests. Wilson Jones's and Robert Criner's testimony demonstrates that Black witnesses in Madison County actively and independently assessed white neighbors' wartime political conduct, and that the federal claims process depended on, but did not reciprocally compensate, Black legal knowledge.
Questions: Can Wilson Jones (Colored) be traced in the 1870/1880 Madison County census or Freedmen's Bureau records? What was Robert Criner's status (enslaved vs. free) during the war? Is there a genealogical link between Seaborn Jones and Alexander P. Jones that explains any shared Avalon-area landholding?

Document Title: "The Negroes and the Juries" -- Selma Times-Journal (reprinted from Tuskaloosa Times), Feb. 16, 1884, p.3
Source: Newspapers.com, The Selma Times-Journal (Selma, Alabama), Sat. Feb. 16, 1884, p.3 -- https://www.newspapers.com/image/571502744/
Evidence: Reports that on a Saturday in early 1884, a committee of Black men from Tuscaloosa County -- named as Lawrence Weaver, Fortentius Williams, and Thornton McGuire -- "headed" a delegation from a county meeting of "colored people" and formally petitioned Probate Judge Browne, asking why Black men (who worked the roads and paid taxes) were excluded from jury service despite being "as good and as competent to serve" as many white jurors from the hills. The judge cited Alabama Code Section 4733, which left jury-list selection to the discretion of the probate judge, sheriff, and circuit clerk based on their own judgment of "competence," "intelligence," and "fair character." The committee then made the same appeal to the sheriff and circuit clerk, receiving the same answer.
Why It Is Important: Documents organized, collective Black civic advocacy for jury service just eight years after the end of Reconstruction -- a direct act of institution-building and rights-claiming testing the discretionary, race-neutral-on-its-face statutory language that in practice was used to exclude Black citizens from juries. Strongly relevant to the paper's H7 (Black agency/Reconstruction/institution-building) and H2 (legal/archival erasure via facially neutral statutes) themes.
Connections: Lawrence Weaver; Fortentius Williams; Thornton McGuire; Probate Judge Browne; Alabama Code Section 4733 (1876); Tuscaloosa County
Conclusions: This is Tuscaloosa County, not Madison County -- geographically outside the immediate Avalon/Huntsville focus, but directly relevant as comparative evidence for the broader Alabama legal-erasure and Black-agency themes the paper draws on for sociological/legal context.
Questions: Was this committee tied to any formal civic or political organization (Union League, church, etc.)? Did any of the three named men appear in other Reconstruction-era Alabama records? Was Alabama Code Section 4733 challenged in court, and with what outcome?

Document Title: 2020 and the Future of Alabama History: The Avalon Plantation Marker Story (transcript)
Source: Alabama Historical Association (AHA) virtual panel, Nov. 10, 2020; featuring Dr. Christine Sears (UAH), Drew Adan & Vaughn Bocchino (UAH researchers), Mark Wilson (AHA Secretary), Scotty Kirkland (Alabama Dept. of Archives & History)
Evidence: Full panel transcript describing UAH's Avalon Plantation Marker research project. Confirms: Lewellen Jones (Rev. War veteran, land in GA and Limestone Co. AL) bought Avalon 1820, died within ~3 months; estate divided between two sons; Alexander Jones inherited Avalon plus half the enslaved people. Enslaved population grew from 20 (1820) to 139 by the 1850 census under Alexander Jones. Post-Civil-War owners Priscilla Holmes Drake and James Perry Drake (from Indiana, suffragists) owned Avalon c.1868-1871; sold portions of land to descendants of Avalon's enslaved population, including Shandy and Reuben Jones. On Lewellen Jones's 1820 death, enslaved woman Eliza Jones and her three biracial children were manumitted (researchers speculate father was Alexander Jones or Lewellen Jones - labeled speculation, not fact). Shandy Jones grew up a literate free man of color in Alabama. Reuben Jones (Shandy's half-brother), born on Avalon Plantation, was a 1870-census neighbor of William Hooper Councill; Freedmen's Bureau records show Councill taught at the 'Jones School' in a building owned by Reuben Jones (c.1869-1870) on Avalon Plantation (now UAH campus). 2018 ground-penetrating radar survey (Ben Hoksbergen archaeology class) found anomalies consistent with grave sites, proposed as enslaved cemetery location (unconfirmed as of 2020). Three-marker plan described: (1) Jones Cemetery/general history marker behind Morton Hall, (2) slave village/Jones School/birthplace of Shandy & Reuben Jones marker, (3) pending enslaved cemetery marker.
Why It Is Important: Directly corroborates and expands the core Avalon/Jones/Drake/Shandy-Reuben Jones/Jones School narrative from an independent, citable, dated public-history source (AHA + UAH researchers), including specific census figures (20 enslaved in 1820 -> 139 by 1850) and the William Hooper Councill/Freedmen's Bureau connection to the Jones School.
Connections: Lewellen Jones; Alexander Jones; Eliza Jones (manumitted 1820); Shandy Jones; Reuben Jones; Priscilla Holmes Drake; James Perry Drake; William Hooper Councill; Jones School; Freedmen's Bureau; Ben Hoksbergen (archaeology); Dr. Christine Sears; Drew Adan; Vaughn Bocchino
Conclusions: Independent scholarly/public-history confirmation of Avalon's Jones-Drake ownership chain and the Shandy/Reuben Jones manumission and post-emancipation community (Jones School) narrative. The 1850 census figure of 139 enslaved persons under Alexander Jones is a new specific data point to verify against the actual 1850 slave schedule. CORRECTION (2026-09-24): the transcript's '20 in 1820' figure is superseded — Lewellen Jones's probate inventory, taken 19 Oct 1820, lists '47 Negroes' (Madison County Probate Record Book 2, pp. 153-154, Estate of Lewellen Jones, Case No. 223); the will splits the residue equally between the two sons (minus the $2,000 equalizer), not 'Avalon + half to Alexander'; and Lewellen died before the 7 Aug 1820 census day, so the figure was never a census count. The documented number is 47. See DB1 1658-1659; DB4 661.
Questions: Need to verify: (1) exact name of the suffrage organization Priscilla Holmes Drake served as officer in (transcript excerpt cuts off), (2) primary-source citation for the 139-enslaved 1850 figure (which slave schedule/page), (3) whether the enslaved cemetery was ever archaeologically confirmed after 2020, (4) full name/details of the two graduate students mentioned as starting descendant-tracing research in 2021, (5) original publication URL/venue for this transcript.

Panelists: Christine Sears, Drew Adan, Vaughn Bocchino (University of Alabama in Huntsville); Mark Wilson (AHA); Scotty Kirkland (Alabama Dept. of Archives & History). Document Title: July 1847 Elbert A. Thompson letter to Dr. John Young Bassett re "Ellick Jones" note and Texas land exchange, and finding aid, John Young Bassett Papers #1527-z
Document Type: Primary source: original manuscript letter (digitized scan) + archival finding aid
Source: Southern Historical Collection, Wilson Special Collections Library, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill; John Young Bassett Papers, #1527-z, Z Box 78, Folder 3 (letter) and Folder 1 (finding aid)
Evidence: Letter dated Matagorda, Texas, July 15/18 1847, from Elbert A. Thompson to "Dr Bassett" (Dr. John Young Bassett of Huntsville, Alabama), postmarked Matagorda, Texas, July 19. Thompson discusses the insolvent estate of his late brother Dr. Asa Watkins Thompson, whose debts exceed its assets, and proposes settling debts by exchanging land in western Texas (then cheap, near San Antonio). He writes: "Ellick Jones holds a note against the Estate for near $1500 which was due in 1836 -- I would willingly exchange him land for it, at one dollar per acre... perhaps he would be willing to give the note for one or two thousand acres," routed via an intermediary "of New Orleans," and asks Bassett to make "no mention of this matter." He also references a dispute with his sister Nancy over the elder Thompsons' estate settlement, to be resolved by arbitration. Signed "Your friend, Elbert A. Thompson." The accompanying finding aid (SHC #1527-z, John Y. Bassett Papers, 1822-1871, 153 items, donated by Mrs. Edward Turnbull/Lenore Bassett Young of Huntsville, Sept. 1948) corroborates an Aug. 15, 1843 letter from brother-in-law Robert J. Manning re financial affairs/investments in Texas, and twelve letters of 1842-43 pertaining to settlement of the estate of Mrs. John Y. Bassett's deceased parents (Asa and Polly Thompson) from A. R. Manning of Demopolis, Alabama.
Why It Is Important: Directly ties "Ellick Jones" of Madison County, Alabama -- hypothesized to be Alexander P. Jones -- to a $1,500 promissory note held since 1836 against the insolvent estate of Dr. Asa Watkins Thompson, and to a proposed 1847 exchange of western Texas land in settlement. First primary source located placing Alexander P. (2) 'Verrel, John,' 9 Dec. 1817, Dinwiddie County: 'Attorney in fact for Lewellin Jones, commander the 4th company in the 1st Virginia Regiment of Light Dragoons during the Revolutionary War, asks for compensation for his services.' Jones and others during the Revolutionary War asks for a pension.' Box 53, Folder 52, Film 38. (5) 'Jones, Lewellyn,' 6 Dec. 1827, Miscellaneous (Chronological): 'Administrator John Hamlin, deceased, asks for an act authorizing the sale of Hamlin's unprofitable slaves.' Box 297, Folder 116, Film 235. (6) 'Jones, Lewellyn,' no date, Miscellaneous (Alphabetical), Order: 'Order that a bill be brought in with the petition of Lewellyn Jones, administrator of John Hamlin, deceased.' Box 304, Folder 5, Film 240.

The project brief flagged Georgia as a plausible but undocumented theatre of family business; this converts it into a documented one. Oglethorpe County sits in the Georgia upcountry cotton belt -- precisely the migration corridor Virginia planters used before pushing on into the Tennessee Valley and north Alabama after the land openings of 1806-1819. The chronology also fits our Lewellen Jones (d. 1820, Bedford Co., Va., probate no. 223) far better than pension W7906 does: he petitions in person in 1808, then through an attorney-in-fact in 1817 and 1818 -- the standard arrangement for a claimant who is elderly, out of state, or both -- and the claim falls silent after 1818, two years before our man's death.

The 1827 Hamlin petition is itself a record about enslaved people -- a request for legislative authority to sell 'Hamlin's unprofitable slaves' -- so the underlying file should name individuals.
Conclusions: Documented fact that these index entries exist and read as quoted. Identifying the Oglethorpe County captain WITH our Lewellen Jones of Bedford County is a strong, well-motivated HYPOTHESIS, not a proven fact. The 1827 Hamlin petitioner postdates our man's 1820 death and is therefore a different, probably younger Lewellyn Jones -- possibly a son or nephew.

Document Title: Virginia bounty-land file VAS1302, Capt. Lewellin Jones -- four warrants totaling 4,000 acres issued 8 Sept. 1804, VERIFYING the family memoir's '1804 land bounty' claim
Document Type: State bounty-land and military claim file (transcribed; original in Virginia Land Office records)
Source: Virginia Land Office / Executive Department, file VAS1302, transcribed by Will Graves at revwarapps.org
Evidence: Independent, decisive corroboration of the Legislative Petitions entries. The file styles him 'Lewellin Jones,' 'Lewelling Jones,' 'Leulin Jones,' and 'Lewelling Jones of Amelia.' RANK AND UNIT: senior captain in the 1st Regiment of Horse raised in Virginia on the Continental establishment in 1776, commanding the 4th Company, 1st Virginia Regiment of Light Dragoons, under Maj. Theodorick Bland as commandant; served until late 1779 or early 1780; three and a half years' service. GEORGIA: 'Lewellin Jones of the County of Oglethorpe in the State of Georgia'; he executed his POWER OF ATTORNEY at Oglethorpe, Georgia, on 6 APRIL 1804; the petition states his removal to Georgia 'was considered necessary to repair a fortune injured, if not entirely ruined, by sacrifices made during the struggle for independence.' LAND BOUNTY: four warrants issued 8 SEPT. 1804 to 'the Representative of Lewellin Jones' -- no. 5063 (2,000 acres), no. 5064 (500), no. 5065 (400), no. 5066 (1,100), TOTAL 4,000 ACRES -- directed to the Principal Surveyor of the lands set apart for Virginia's officers and soldiers; copy certified 19 Dec. 1816 by William G. Pendleton, Register of the Virginia Land Office. AFFIANTS AND OFFICIALS: Charles Stainback and John Evans (both sworn in NOTTOWAY COUNTY before Thomas J. Cocke, J.P., 30 Aug. 1804, both stating they served WITH him); Buller Claiborne (2 July 1804); Col. Robert Lawson, formerly of the 4th Virginia Regiment (30 June 1804), calling him 'a brave and faithful officer'; John Crawford, who knew 'Lewelling Jones, of Amelia' and saw him on duty 'to the northward' in 1777-78; John Verrel / Verrell, 'Attorney in Fact for Lewellin Jones'; Samuel Coleman; John Gaurranty. His original captain's commission was exhibited among the vouchers. Independently, the Friends of Valley Forge regimental roster lists 'Captain Lewellen Jones' among the company commanders of the 1st Light Dragoon Regiment, which entered Valley Forge with 136 men assigned and 115 fit for duty.
Why It Is Important: This VERIFIES the specific detail that made DB1 row 336's family memoir look unreliable. The memoir claimed 'Capt. Lewellen Jones's Revolutionary War service and 1804 land bounty.' Both halves are now documented from state records: the captaincy is attested by a former colonel and by two men who served with him, and the land bounty is an exact date match -- 4,000 acres in four warrants on 8 September 1804. The memoir's separate tradition that the Joneses wintered at Valley Forge also matches, since the 1st Light Dragoons were a Valley Forge regiment. A researcher should treat the memoir as a flawed but substantially grounded source rather than discard it.
Connections: AMELIA AND NOTTOWAY ARE NOW CENTRAL, AND THIS CORRECTS DB1 row 430. Nottoway County was formed from Amelia County in 1789. The captain is called 'of Amelia,' and his supporting affidavits were sworn in Nottoway. In row 430 I ruled out a 'Lewellen Jones of Nottoway' (Jackson elector, 1824) as an unrelated man. That dismissal now needs reopening: a Nottoway Lewellen Jones is far more likely to be the captain's kin, or the captain's own successor in name, than an unrelated coincidence. Also note the phrase 'the Representative of Lewellin Jones' on all four warrants, which may indicate he was already deceased or acting only through his agent by 1804 -- this must be resolved, because it bears directly on whether the captain can be our man who died in 1820.
Conclusions: Documented fact as to the contents of file VAS1302 as transcribed, the warrant numbers, acreages, and the 8 Sept. 1804 issue date. CAUTION: this is a TRANSCRIPTION, not a document image, and must be verified against the original Land Office records. CAUTION: 'of Amelia' conflicts with our man's Bedford County residence and death; the identification is not settled. CAUTION: the transcriber's own footnotes flag that affiants Buller Claiborne and John Evans cannot be matched to any other pensioned veteran of those names.
Questions: Does 'the Representative of Lewellin Jones' mean the captain was dead by Sept. 1804? If so, who was the representative, and can the captain be our Lewellen Jones at all? Where were warrants 5063-5066 actually located and surveyed -- Kentucky's Virginia Military District, or the Ohio lands? Do Amelia and Nottoway County records document his family? Is the 1824 Nottoway elector of DB1 row 430 a son?

Document Title: John Nelson Spotswood Jones's Law Office as the Site of Huntsville's First Public Library (1818-1819) -- corroborated by two independent sources
Document Type: Secondary source (local history), corroborated across two independent publications
Source: (1) Paul A. Hays, From Carnegie to Fort Book: The History of the Huntsville-Madison County Public Library; (2) Huntsville Historical Review, Vol. 44, No. 2 (Fall/Winter 2019), Huntsville-Madison County Historical Society
Evidence: In July 1818 Dr. Thomas Fearn wrote to Clement Clay urging the creation of a subscription library in Huntsville, then still Alabama Territory; a meeting followed and roughly $2,000-3,000 was subscribed. The Huntsville Library Company issued shares (e.g., Share No. 59 to William Atwood, $20, dated 10 Dec. 1818, signed Robert Fearn, Treasurer, and Thomas G. Percy, President). The library was for men-subscribers only. Books were first assumed to be housed in Mr. Minor's office in the courthouse, but 'the law office of John Nelson Spotswood Jones is credited with the location of the first library in October 1819, as Jones opened his law office in September 1819.' A newspaper notice of the era states: 'the Books are opened at the office of J. N. S. Jones, Esq. next door to the Printing Office on the street leading to Ditto's Landing [current Madison & Whitesburg],' open Tuesdays and Fridays 11:30 AM-12:30 PM, John Boardman, Librarian. The HHR Vol. 44 No. 2 article independently confirms: 'The library, for gentlemen only, was located in the Madison Street law office of John Nelson Spotswood Jones and opened on Tuesdays and Thursdays while Jones was out to lunch,' and notes it was the first public library in the Alabama Territory. A replica of the Jones law office stands today in Constitution Village, Huntsville, facing Madison Street next to the Boardman printing building.
Why It Is Important: This is a significant, independently-corroborated civic-history fact directly tying a founding-era Jones-family member (already tracked in this database in connection with the Madison County Jones/Perkins civic elite, cf. DB1 row 451) to a specific, still-commemorated physical site and civic institution in Huntsville -- the first public library in the entire Alabama Territory. It is directly relevant to the project's 'institutional knowledge/public memory' research angle: the library was subscription-only (for paying gentlemen), illustrating how Huntsville's earliest civic and cultural institutions were built by and for a small propertied white elite in a county whose wealth depended on enslaved labor.
Connections: John Nelson Spotswood Jones (Madison County founding-era Jones/Perkins elite, DB1 row 451); Dr. Thomas Fearn; Clement Clay; Robert Fearn; Thomas G. Percy; John Boardman; Constitution Village, Huntsville.
Conclusions: Two independent secondary sources corroborate the same underlying fact (Jones's law office as the first library site, Sept./Oct. 1819), which strengthens confidence in the fact itself, though both ultimately likely draw on the same underlying 1818-1819 newspaper notices as their primary source.

Document Title: Correspondence: the 1840 ‘mortgage one of the Children’ letter, the 1842 judgment letter, and the 1853 boarding-house letter
Document Type: Verified finding — three letters in the file, one torn
Source: 14 Dec 1840, Manchester: Elizabeth Jones to Samuel G. Berry (img 218, ARK 33S7-9BQW-WM2, visually read; docketed Exhibit F); May 1842: Elizabeth Jones to S. B. Jackson (img 185, ARK 33S7-8BQH-DTT; answer’s Exhibit A); 24 Aug 1846: Samuel G. Berry to Elizabeth (img 224); 26 Jan 1853, New Market: Samuel G. Berry to Rev. Evidence: 1840 (Verified): ‘I am well as to health but distressed in mind John Bell has pushed on me for the money and had to mortgage one of the Children for the money and have it to pay by Christmas or lose the Child dont fail to fetch me the money before that time… P.S. the debt amounts to $87.50’ — signed ‘your needy Aunt… E. Jones.’ The mortgaged child was Jesse (image 76). 1842 (Verified): asks S. B. Jackson to send ~$35 ‘to pay off the Judgement which is about thirty Dollers and cost.’ 1846 (Verified): Samuel writes his aunt — sickness about, money not to be had ‘not under [?] per cent,’ hopes someone will ‘let you Have the money to pay John Bell.’ 1853 (Verified): Samuel warns Rev. Lunsford that ‘my aunt Mrs Betsey Jones has left my protection’ and is boarding at his house — board her at his own risk; don’t look to ‘the Horse that she has with her.’ 1839 (Fenced): an unsigned, bottom-torn letter from a nephew/niece — ‘I acted vary mean with you about that letter,’ John Beary and Josiah Beary charging $50 each, ‘uncle John,’ money ‘verry scarse in this country’ — writer’s name lost with the torn edge.

Document Title: RULED OUT: the Columbus/Reuben-as-Elizabeth's-sons claim (2026-09-21, four-objection case)
Source: H&D 2026 (oral history + the scholarship's own age objection); Columbus's Freedman's Bank register No. 29, Oct 2, 1867 (pixel-verified: mother Eliza Jones, father Turner Moore); Reuben's register No. 1406, Dec 24, 1872 (parent names CONTESTED — H&D fn 19 says Turner Moore/Eliza Jones, image pass reads father Simon/mother Eliza, pixel audit pending); ACT-1820 (the four-person family); SJR25
Evidence: I am ruling this one out as stated, and I am keeping the oral-history claim visible while I do it — the family remembers it this way and that deserves respect, but the documents won't carry it. Objection one is the scholarship's own: Elizabeth, born about 1780, would have been about 47 at Columbus's birth and about 53 at Reuben's, with younger siblings documented as late as 1843 when she would have been about 63 — Hoksbergen and DeNeefe call it 'remote.' Objection two is ours and it is the strongest: Columbus's own register (No. 29, pixel-verified) names his mother as Eliza Jones and his father as Turner Moore — a named father where the claim needs an unknown one, and a mother whose name does not match Elizabeth. (Reuben's register is contested on the father's name — see col C — so this objection as stated rests on Columbus's register; if the pixel audit confirms Simon as Reuben's father, the brothers are maternal half-brothers sharing Eliza.) Objection three: Columbus told the bank in 1867 he had been 'once a slave,' with children born 1847–1853 on the Madison plantation — the shape of enslaved birth, not of a free child of a woman manumitted in 1820. Objection four: the 1820 statute defines Elizabeth's family as mother plus Evelina, Ann, and Shandy — no other children appear in the emancipation record or in Shandy's descendant literature. Ruled out as currently stated. The claim stays fenced as a claim, with the objections beside it.
Why It Is Important: The claim lives in family memory and in the scholarship's shadow — the project has to state its position plainly rather than let the ambiguity stand.

Document Title: Mary Stith's freed community, Lot 17 — will (Dec 15, 1813; recorded Williamsburg Hustings Court Feb 26, 1816): 'All the coloured people in my family being born my slaves, but now liberated' + bequests
Document Type: Verified — the will survived in Robert Anderson's business papers
Evidence: Mary Stith (daughter of William Stith, College president 1752–55, and Judith Randolph of Tuckahoe; never married) was a Williamsburg slaveholder 1769–1815, then an emancipator. Her will (Dec 15, 1813; recorded Williamsburg Hustings Court Feb 26, 1816): "All the coloured people in my family being born my slaves, but now liberated, I think it my duty not to leave them destitute nor leave them unrecompensed for past services rendered to me." Bequests: dwelling house + lot + £100 to Jenny, "the mother of the family"; tin shop + £25 each to granddaughters Jenny Gillett and Patty Gillett; "my house on the main street called Woods shop" to Nelly Bolling and "her two sisters Eve and Sally" (£50/£25/£25). Residue to "my relation jenny Westwood daughter of William Westwood deceased, late of the town of Hampton" (white relation, not enslaved). Estate settlement (Robert Anderson's papers) gives married names: "To Cash paid Eve Mitchells legacy" → Eve Mitchell; "To Cash paid Sally Skinner legacy" → Sally Skinner. Document Title: James Anderson's armory, Lot 18 — enslaved and hired Black labor: Nat sold $600 at the Nov 1, 1803 estate sale (buyer appears Robert Anderson); 1779 hire ad ('six likely young NEGRO FELLOWS for six months' at £100 each); Day Book Apr 26, 1779 '10 Yds d o for approns for the Negroes hired by the Publick'; Dec 1777 contract £32/month for nine hands; state-owned slaves and five apprentice nailors after 1778–79; Moody rented five enslaved people from William Moody Jr. early 1779 (£111, state-paid)

Evidence: "Nat, a Negro man blacksmith / 600.00 / Robert Anderson / 600.00" — sold at James Anderson's estate sale, Nov 1, 1803 (two-column table; buyer appears to be Robert Anderson) — two-column layout needs manuscript confirmation. 1779 hire ad: "I WILL give extraordinary wages to a good BLACKSMITH and NAILER, that is capable of acting as foreman in my shops.--I am in want of six likely young NEGRO FELLOWS for six months, for which I will give 100£. each." The hires materialized: "April 26, 1779 / To 48 Yds baize @ / 10 Yds d o for approns for the Negroes hired by the Publick / 36.-.- / Recd by James Anderson" (Day Book, Public Armoury). After the 1778–79 enlargement, Anderson "increased his labor force by acquiring the use of state owned slaves and five apprentice nailors" (Public Store Day Book). Philip Moody "rented five enslaved people from his cousin William Moody, Jr. for two months at the beginning of 1779, with the state footing the £111 bill."
Why It Is Important: This is the hard evidence of enslaved and hired Black labor at the Block 10 armory — Nat the blacksmith by name, the state's £100-per-head hiring, and the apron-cloth entry proving the 1779 hires actually arrived. Anderson's shop ran on public money and Black labor.

Document Title: 1835-007 — Administrator of Armstead Minor v. Executor of Thomas V. Jones: Margana, Jim, Mary — full firsthand read
Document Type: Chancery court case file — full firsthand read (46 pages)
Source: Library of Virginia, Bedford County chancery causes 1835-007; images read in the 2026-09-22 unrendered sweep (builds on DB1 row 489’s cover-sheet read)
Evidence: Three enslaved people named, all in the deed of trust of June 14, 1832 (Armstead Minor → trustee William L. Goggin, securing a $180.30 bond debt to Thomas V. Jones; acknowledged by all three parties before Robt. Mitchell, Clerk): Margana (“a woman,” ~16–17), Jim (“a boy”), Mary (“a girl”) — plus “their future increase.” Margana was the only one sold: at the trustee sale on November 24, 1832 at the courthouse door in Liberty, Thomas V. Jones bought her himself for $300 as the highest bidder; the auction was cried by plaintiff Daniel Aunspaugh at the trustee’s request. Jones publicly declared on the sale day that she was unsound. Joseph Andrews deposed he would have bid $320–325 had she been in good health, calling her “a very likely girl.” The sale was advertised two weeks in a Lynchburg newspaper per the deed’s terms. The bill’s fraud narrative — that Jones contracted privately with the widow to pay $325 and not sell under the deed, then sold anyway — is Verified as what the bill alleges; the answer denies any promise to forbear and says Jones found her unsound and $300 fair. Explicit negative: no other enslaved person is named in the 46 pages. “Mary” here is NOT the 1805 note’s “Mary Ann” — flagged non-match, not a lead.
Why It Is Important: A fully-read Bedford case naming three enslaved people with prices, ages, and a fraud dispute around the sale — exactly the kind of documentation that shows how enslaved people moved through debt and trust instruments. Margana is a named, priced, health-described woman; Jim and Mary are named but undescribed.

Document Title: 1859-030 — Chapman S. Jones v. Creasy & Bennett: Parthenia, Jim, Betty, Munch/Monroe — full firsthand read and name adjudication
Document Type: Chancery court case file — full firsthand read (16 pages; double-read by two agents)
Source: Library of Virginia, Bedford County chancery causes 1859-030; images read in the 2026-09-22 unrendered sweep (builds on DB1 row 499’s cover-sheet read)
Evidence: On June 16, 1858 Chapman S. Jones bought four enslaved people from Tandy K. Jones for $1,200 and took possession. Constable William A. Creasy then levied on the four as Tandy K. Jones’s property under three executions issued in the Commonwealth’s name against Samuel H. Quarles (sheriff of Bedford) and his official-bond securities (including Tandy K. Jones), and advertised them for sale Monday, September 27, 1858, at Liberty. Chapman’s bill (sworn September 25, 1858) sought an injunction; Judge George W. Gilmer awarded it on a $4,000 bond (obligors: Chapman S. Jones, Robert C. Jones, Samuel D. Jones, John H. Jones, Daniell P. Jones). Chapman died before final hearing; the cause was revived in the name of John H. Jones, administrator c.t.a.; final decree October 4, 1859: the injunction was made perpetual — the four were protected from the execution sale. The four, consistent across all five naming documents — Parthenia (woman, ~34), Jim (~10), Betty (~8), Munch/Monroe (~9). ADJUDICATION: a parallel extraction had rendered the woman’s name “Caroline”/“Carolina”/“Katherina” in three documents; a 300-DPI letter-by-letter re-read of all 16 pages found no such variants anywhere — “Parthenia” is the sole spelling. Document Title: 1890 Huntsville: a colored ward sending two Black aldermen - Charles Jones and Lucien Ware - to the City Council
Document Type: Secondary - Huntsville history volume, chapter 2 (Political Expression), p.16, with newspaper footnotes
Source: Huntsville history volume, ch.2, p.16 (CamScanner 6-19-26 21.18_1.JPG); footnotes: The Weekly Independent, April 8, 1892 (nn.61-62); The Weekly Mercury, February 25, 1891 (nn.63, 65); March 4, 1891 (n.64); book title unverified from scan, tentatively Elizabeth Humes Chapman, Changing Huntsville, 1890-1899
Evidence: Amazing to the uninitiated investigator is that in 1890 there was in Huntsville a colored ward sending two Negro aldermen to the City Council. Charles Jones and Lucien Ware, colored, worked on committees with W. R. Van Valkenburg, J. R. Stegall, and John G. Baker, whites. They not only worked on committees but discussed situations and policies as freely, if not as frequently, as their white associates. They reported on public opinion in their wards as the white men reported public opinion in theirs. They appointed officers to work in their wards. Jackson, son of James Jackson, who acted as his father's general agent under a verbal/power of attorney (lost or destroyed). James Jackson's deposition states he executed the October 24, 1840 mortgage to Dearing, moved the enslaved people from the Western District of Tennessee to North Alabama in 1832, inherited them from his father except Aggy (given by his wife's uncle) and Edward (bought in Jefferson County, Georgia, 1816/1817); that he gave Dr. Jackson no special authority to sell Solomon and Hercules but a general power of attorney; that he intended to transfer 16 shares of Georgia Rail Road & Banking Company stock (par $1,600, saleable for at least $1,200 at Athens) to Dearing; and that Dr. Jackson sold Solomon & Hercules to Col. J. F. Lightfoot for valuable consideration. Dr. Henry M. Jackson testified Lightfoot bought the boys in January 1842 for about $1,000 by assuming James Jackson's debts (about $800: one to Paul J. Watkins, one to J. J. McMahan & Co.), plus about $200 paid to Jackson's use; and that Dearing twice (Jan. & May 1841, at Dearing's Lawrence County plantation and at Dearing's house in Athens, Georgia) told him the proper course was to sell part or all of the mortgaged enslaved people. The jury found for the defendant; judgment entered Sept term 1847 that defendant go hence without day and recover his costs. James Jackson further stated he was a certified bankrupt discharged by the U.S. Bankrupt Court for Georgia. The mortgage also covered Tilla (sold to John M. Swoope) and Fenton (sold to Paul J. Walkins) by special direction of Dr. H. M. Jackson.

Document Title: Priscilla Holmes Buell Drake and James Perry Drake: identification, Indiana backstory, and the 1868–1871 Avalon window
Source: Wikipedia (dates/offices, secondary); Wikisource, "Woman of the Century/Priscilla Holmes Drake" (1893 profile; New Harmony/Owen/Mott details); Alexander Street biographical sketch of daughter Annie Buell Drake Robertson (Apr. 5, 1880 petition); Drew Adan, "The Avalon Plantation Marker Story," AHA 2020 transcript (ownership window); UAH marker article
Evidence: Priscilla Holmes Buell Drake (June 18, 1812, Ithaca, NY – Feb 11, 1892, Huntsville, AL; buried Maple Hill Cemetery): suffragist; only Alabama representative to the National Woman Suffrage Association in the 1860s; officer of the NWSA; worked with Robert Dale Owen at the Indiana Constitutional Convention (1850–51) on removing women's legal disabilities; lifelong friend and correspondent of Lucretia Mott; the only woman present at Lucy Stone's first Indianapolis lecture; with daughter Annie and others petitioned the U.S. House for women's suffrage (Apr. 5, 1880). James Perry Drake (Sept 15, 1797, Robeson County, NC – Aug 12, 1876, Huntsville, AL; buried Maple Hill Cemetery): lawyer; Indiana General Assembly (1848–49); Indiana State Treasurer (1850–53); founder of Lebanon, Indiana; colonel, 1st Indiana Volunteers (Mexican-American War); DEMOCRAT; farmer. Uncle of Union Gen. Don Carlos Buell (Priscilla's nephew); father-in-law of Union Gen. William T. H. Brooks. Moved to NEAR HUNTSVILLE, ALABAMA, IN 1861; continued suffrage work. Owned Avalon c. 1868–1871 (Drew Adan, AHA 2020 transcript: "they only owned Avalon very briefly from about 1868 to 1871"), purchasing after the 1867 death of Alexander S. Perkins; sold the main plantation and house to the Crawfords; parceled smaller tracts to descendants of the enslaved. Indiana backstory ("Woman of the Century" profile): James Drake was "brought into intimate business and social relations with the New Harmony Community, under the Rapps, father and son, and when their possessions were transferred to the SCOTCH PHILANTHROPIST, ROBERT OWEN, he naturally held the same relations with the Owen association."

Document Title: The Drake verdicts: parceling for SALE not gift; abolitionism NOT supported; the Owen 'philanthropist' contamination
Document Type: Analytic verdicts on tested claims (secondary analysis of primary-adjacent evidence)
Source: Well-land-drake-report.md Target 4 (2026-09-23); H&D 2026 fns 73–74, 77, 81; UAH marker article; AHA 2020 transcript
Evidence: CLAIM (a) — PHILANTHROPY, TESTED, PARTLY SUPPORTED WITH A MAJOR CORRECTION. SUPPORTED: the Drakes did transfer former plantation land to formerly enslaved people — BY SALE, documented: Reuben Jones bought parcels from the Drakes in January 1871 (Deed Books TT p. 488; UU p. 350; DB1 rows 1521–1522). Drew Adan (AHA 2020 transcript): "they also portioned up smaller areas of the land and sold those off to descendants of the enslaved population that was at Avalon, including Shandy and Reuben Jones." UAH's marker article: "The Drakes facilitated parceling portions of the former plantation FOR SALE to the emancipated Jones slaves." An 1874 trustee sale of "Drake land" bounded "north by Wesley Jones's land" (DB1 row 1130) corroborates the parceling pattern in the deed record. THE CORRECTION: this was parceling for sale, NOT giving land back. No gift, donation, or below-market conveyance is documented. "Philanthropist" in the Drake network attaches most directly to ROBERT OWEN ("the Scotch philanthropist") — the Drakes' ASSOCIATE, not the Drakes themselves. Family-lore contamination risk identified: the "philanthropist" label may have migrated from Owen (via the New Harmony connection both Drakes held) onto the Drakes, then inflated "sold parcels to freedpeople" into "gave land back to freed slaves." The documented facts support: reformers who sold land to freedpeople. They do NOT support: philanthropists giving land back. CLAIM (b) — ABOLITIONISM, TESTED, NOT SUPPORTED. No documented anti-slavery activity by either Drake was found. What is documented is women's-SUFFRAGE activism (Priscilla, extensively; James as her political partner — "for many years, the women's suffrage movement in Alabama was represented only by Priscilla Holmes Drake and her husband"). Adjacent-but-not-equivalent facts that must not be blurred: Priscilla's friendship/correspondence with Lucretia Mott (a genuine abolitionist) and her parlor work with Robert Dale Owen (author of the abolitionist text The Wrong of Slavery, 1864) — on women's legal disabilities, NOT slavery. Association with abolitionists is not abolitionism. Counter-indicator: the Drakes moved to Alabama — a SLAVE STATE — IN 1861, at the outbreak of the Civil War. James P. Drake's party affiliation was DEMOCRATIC (antebellum Indiana Democrat, officeholder under Jackson/Monroe patronage networks) — the party of slavery's defense nationally in that era. Verdict: suffragists and social reformers — yes, solidly documented. Post-war land sales to freedpeople — yes, documented. Abolitionists — no evidence found; the label should not be used.
Why It Is Important: This is the verdict the Drake lead existed to produce: the user's feeling was half-right — something real is there (the parceling), but it is post-war reformist land dealing, not abolitionism and not philanthropy-in-the-giving sense. This protects the paper from the two most tempting overclaims in the Drake network and names the exact contamination pathway (Owen → Drakes) so the label migration doesn't creep back in. UAH's 2020s publications present the Drakes as "wellknown social reformers and women suffragists" (Adan) — the institution's current narrative leans on the reformer framing, which this verdict confirms while fencing the inflation.
Connections: Priscilla Holmes Buell Drake; James Perry Drake; Robert Owen; Robert Dale Owen; Lucretia Mott; Reuben Jones; Shandy Jones (Drake purchase asserted, deed unverified); Wesley Jones (DB1 row 1130 boundary); Crawford family; Lucretia Mott; NWSA
Conclusions: The Drakes are inside the documented Avalon-to-UAH title story as brief transitional owners — but as parcelers-by-sale, not as institutional founders and not as abolitionists. Document Title: The Jones School, 1869–1870: the Bureau reports name it, and the rent shifted from Reuben to Crawford in January 1870
Document Type: Primary-source-anchored scholarship (H&D 2026, citing Freedmen's Bureau Teacher's Monthly School Reports)
Source: Hoksbergen & DeNeefe 2026, Alabama Review 79(3), pp. 216–217, fns 78–82; Freedmen's Bureau, Teacher's Monthly School Reports, March 1869–March 1870 (cited copies on file at Environmental Management Division, Dept. of Public Works, Garrison–Redstone Arsenal, Huntsville, AL); 1870 U.S. Federal Census, Madison County, AL, NARA M593, p. 13
Evidence: The March 1869–March 1870 school is documented in the PRIMARY record, not family lore: the Freedmen's Bureau Teacher's Monthly School Reports show Councill teaching the "JONES SCHOOL" and paying rent first to Reuben Jones, then — from JANUARY 1870 — to Thomas B. Crawford. Average attendance: ~39 students. REFINEMENT (changes the established framing): the rent paid TO REUBEN ran March–December 1869 only. From January 1870, rent shifted to Thomas B. Crawford, who had bought the surrounding 138 acres from the Drakes in January 1870 (H&D fn 81). So the "March 1869–March 1870 lease by Reuben" is slightly off: Reuben collected the rent for the first ten months; the school's last three months sat on Crawford-owned ground. This sharpens the thread; it does not contradict it. The lease was a MONTHLY RENTAL OF SPACE, not a recorded deed: no recorded lease instrument in the Madison County deed books has been located or cited anywhere; the evidence is the monthly rent line in the Bureau teacher reports. The Bureau reports themselves are not publicly viewable online in this pass — the cited copies sit at a military-installation office (Redstone Arsenal), not a public archive; free public routes are the NMAAHC Freedmen's Bureau Search Portal and FamilySearch's M810 index (whether the Madison County 1869–70 teacher reports are among the transcribed/indexed pages is Unresolved). Corroboration: the 1870 census (p. 13) places Councill, wife Elizabeth, and infant son William living next door to Reuben and Jane Jones, their two daughters, and Columbus's nineteen-year-old daughter Elizabeth, on the former plantation in Township 4, Range 1 West. School-name note: the Bureau record calls it the "Jones School"; the standard biographies' "Lincoln School, four miles west of Huntsville, in 1868" is very likely the same school under its community name (row 219's Adkins email already logs "Township 3 R 1 West," Lincoln School, and "Jones Place" as name variants) — but the Bureau's March 1869 start date is primary and should be preferred over the secondary 1868. THE PRE-1871 TITLE PUZZLE (evidenced skeleton, still unresolved): Reuben collected monthly school rent March–December 1869 on land he did not own in fee — he bought his Drake parcels in January 1871 (DB1 rows 1521–1522). The Bureau's rent ledger is the title-following evidence: rent to Reuben (Mar–Dec 1869) → rent to Crawford (from Jan 1870), because Crawford bought the surrounding 138 acres from the Drakes in January 1870. The rent followed the fee title — which means the school site lay inside Crawford's 138-acre purchase. Best-supported reading: Reuben, as a formerly-enslaved resident of the former Jones plantation, held the possessory interest (occupant/tenant) and sublet school space; the Bureau paid him as the person in possession. Consistent with his informal claims elsewhere: Reuben asserted "an additional sixty-seven acres just south of Athens Pike in the Northwest Quarter of Section 4, T4S-R1W, although his claim was never formalized with a deed" — in 1874 that parcel was put up for public auction for unpaid taxes assessed to "Reuben Jones and others" (Huntsville Weekly Democrat, Feb 12, 1874; H&D fn 77).
Why It Is Important: This anchors the project's most important institutional thread — Reuben Jones → Councill's 1869 school → the institution that became Alabama A&M — to the primary Bureau record via published scholarship, and it corrects the lease framing in two precise ways: the "Jones School" name and the January 1870 rent shift. The rent-shift is also the cleanest title-chain evidence in the whole 1869–70 puzzle: rent follows fee title. The paper's Jones School section can now be anchored to the Bureau reports via H&D 2026 rather than resting on the project notes alone.
Connections: Reuben Jones (freedman, blacksmith, AL House 1872–73); William Hooper Councill; Thomas B. Crawford; Jane Jones; Elizabeth Councill; Columbus's daughter Elizabeth; Drakes (estate owners c. 1868–1871); Reuben's informal 67-acre claim (NW 1/4 S4 T4S-R1W)
Conclusions: No source found places the schoolroom itself on the plantation — H&D's archaeology note (fn 76) identifies site 1Ma1922 on Reuben's parcel (sheet midden, blacksmithing iron scrap) but does not place the schoolroom. Map it as an approximate area (T4S-R1W, ~3 miles west of Huntsville on Athens Pike), not a pin. Whether "Lincoln School" = "Jones School" is a strong hypothesis with no single source equating them — do not merge the names as proven. The exact 1869 instrument (if any) giving Reuben the possessory interest is Unresolved.

Document Title: After 1875: Reuben's documented hand in A&M — the 1876 'Self Defense' letter and the 1884 industrial-center committee; the Rust fund-holding bridge, 1873–75
Source: Hoksbergen & DeNeefe 2026, pp. 220–221, fns 98–101; Huntsville Advocate, April 6, 1876 (Councill's "Self Defense" letter); Huntsville Independent, October 9, 1884, p. 1; Catalogue of the State Normal School: Huntsville, Alabama, 1883–1884 (Internet Archive; bibliography Section EF); AHA historical marker text (1974)
Evidence: THE INSTITUTIONAL BRIDGE (new, primary): the 1883–84 State Normal School catalogue's "HISTORY AND LOCATION": "In 1873 the Legislature of Alabama appropriated the sum of one thousand dollars to establish a Normal School for colored teachers, at Huntsville. The Institution was placed under the control of three Commissioners, who turned the funds over to the Rust Normal School. It was, therefore, a part of Rust Normal School until May, 1875, when the Commissioners organized the State Normal School for colored students." So the 1873 appropriation (marker: Legislature approved 9 December 1873 "a normal school for the education of colored teachers") was parked inside the Rust Normal School for ~17 months; the separately organized State Normal School under Councill dates to May 1875. But note: this is the RUST school's continuity — NO source found places Councill teaching at Rust in 1870–75 (H&D's account instead stresses the politics: Councill "played into a Democratic ploy for gaining state control of Black higher education in Huntsville by applying to be the first principal," shifting state funds away from Rust — "a normal school which had been established in Huntsville in 1869 with support from the Freedmen's Aid Society and the Northern Methodist Church of Ohio" — which made him "a pariah among many of the educated and politically active African Americans in Huntsville," H&D pp. 220–221). Rust founding-date conflict, preserved with provenance: H&D says 1869 (Freedmen's Aid Society + Northern Methodist Church of Ohio); Wikipedia/Bhamwiki say 1865 (Pittsburg Aid Society) — genuinely conflicting secondary claims; do not pick one. 1870–75 CONTINUITY VERDICT: Councill did NOT teach continuously. His documented 1870–75 record: the mortgaged September 1870 acre (DB1 row 1526); assistant/chief enrolling clerk of the Alabama legislature (1872, 1874); secretary of the Colored National Civil Rights Convention, Washington DC (1873); taught at Morris Brown College, Atlanta (period unspecified); edited the Negro Watchman in Huntsville (1874); ran for the legislature and lost by 176 votes (Nov 3, 1874, H&D p. 220). REUBEN × A&M AFTER 1875 — REAL AND DOCUMENTED AT TWO POINTS: (1) the 1876 Normal School political fight — Councill's "Self Defense" letter in the Huntsville Advocate (April 6, 1876, H&D fn 100) named Reuben Jones among the authors of a character assassination of Councill, while acknowledging Reuben "had been added as an author without his knowledge, possibly to add some clout"; Reuben then supported Councill's reinstatement as principal. (2) In 1884, Reuben was selected for a committee "to plan, locate, and contract construction for a new industrial training center at the Normal School" (Huntsville Independent, October 9, 1884, p. 1; H&D p. 221, fn 101) — the strongest post-1875 document: a direct, dated role in building A&M's industrial program (industrial education added 1878). Industrial-name-date note: 1878 (name change authorized) vs. 1885 ("of Huntsville" form / industrial building constructed) — keep both with the distinction; do not collapse.
Why It Is Important: The 1873–75 gap finally has a documented institutional bridge (the Rust fund-holding) — and an honest break (Councill's 1872–74 record is clerk/political/journalism work, not teaching). Reuben's post-1875 A&M involvement is no longer "no evidence found": the 1884 committee is a concrete, dated, sourced role in A&M's industrial program. This is the other half of the "Reuben × A&M" story the project needs — not just the landlord of 1869, but a builder in 1884. The 1876 letter also shows the texture: Reuben's name used "for clout" without his knowledge, then his support after reinstatement.
Connections: William Hooper Councill; Reuben Jones; Rust Normal School; the three state commissioners (1873); Freedmen's Aid Society; Northern Methodist Church of Ohio / Methodist Episcopal Church / Pittsburg Aid Society (per conflicting accounts); Morris Brown College; Negro Watchman
Conclusions: No evidence of donations, trusteeship, or land conveyance by Reuben to the Normal School/A&M. No evidence his children attended (his daughters' names are not established in the sources reviewed). No legislative education bills: Reuben's House service was the 1872–73 session; the normal-school act was approved December 9, 1873, after he left office — whether he introduced or voted on any education measure in 1872–73 is Unresolved (the Journal of the House, 1872–73, ADAH holdings).

Document Title: Rev. Rowland Jones (1644–1688) — first rector of Bruton Parish; the Tidewater tobacco fortune begins (plantations worked by enslaved labor)

L.’ silver initials and from Orlando naming his only son Lane), mother of Orlando and Anna Maria.

Cary's line — ‘by no means dependent upon his ministerial salary’ — is the cleanest statement of the classic rapid Tidewater enrichment pattern, built on tobacco and enslaved labor.

Document Title: Lane Jones (1707–~1750) — inherited Tidewater estate, tobacco; the 1727 Anne Barber marriage
Source: Cary 1897 — St. Peter's Parish register (birth), marriage record, Henley family Bible memorandum (children's birth dates), Barber/Archer wills; June 15, 1761 York County special verdict and 1763 Cumberland deed via Cary and later scholarship.
Evidence: Born June 15, 1707, St. Peter's Parish, New Kent County, only son of Orlando Jones and Martha Macon. Married 1727 Anne Barber, daughter of Maj. William Barber of York-Hampton Parish (justice of the peace, Burgess 1710, church warden 1703) by his wife Anne Archer — daughter of Capt. James Archer and granddaughter of Elizabeth Hubard Archer (wills proved 1733 and 1726 respectively). Six children (Henley Bible via Cary): Martha (b. May 20, 1728), Anne (b. September 24, 1729), Lane Jr. (b. September 15, 1733), Rowland (‘Rolando,’ b. April 19, 1738), Frances (b. January 26, 1740), William (b. November 7, 1746). A June 15, 1761 special verdict in York County court confirms the same six children — naming Martha Johnson, Anne Hudson, Orlando Jones, Rowland Jones, Frances Barber Jones, and William Jones — plus a granddaughter Anne Barber Jones, ‘daughter and heir of Lain Jones, son of Lain Jones, deceased’ (Lane Jr. died before 1761 leaving an heir). A 1763 Cumberland County deed again groups the heirs: William Johnson and wife Martha; John Hudson and wife Anne; John Jones and Frances Barber Jones, his wife, of Louisa County; Orlando Jones of Albemarle; Rowland Jones of Hanover — five adult shares, two infant shares reserved. Died about 1750.
Why It Is Important: Inheritance and marriage, told plainly: as Orlando's only son he took the core of the Queen's Creek estate, and the 1727 marriage folded the Barber family's standing and the Archer/Hubard kin network into the line. His children were already dispersing west and south — Louisa, Albemarle, Hanover, Cumberland — the family's first step out of the Tidewater core toward the Piedmont frontier.
Connections: Only son of Orlando (row 1761); father of Frances Barber Jones, the corrected link (row 1763); father-in-law of Capt. John Jones (row 1764).
Conclusions: Generation 4: inherited estate plus tobacco plus the Barber/Archer marriage alliance.

Document Title: Capt. John Jones (d. ~1796, intestate, Bedford County) — Llewellyn's father; the Piedmont move and ‘an estate both real and personal to a large amount’
Source: Project Bedford chancery read pass (six cases, 1805–1841); 1966 compiled chart; 1789 Philip Burton receipt (known through the project site and read-pass summary — original not re-read this pass); 1792 Bedford deed (Deed Book T, p. 97 per project notes — not read firsthand this pass).

(Barber) Jones. Children (Bedford chancery read pass): sons Llewellyn Jones and Charles D. Jones; daughters Elizabeth Jones (m. Jesse Anderson) and Nancy T. Jones (m. Nelson Dawson). A 1789 receipt shows Philip Burton receiving £180 Virginia currency plus ten enslaved people as his wife's marriage portion from John Jones — a Burton daughter married into the family, though which of the four named children she was is Unresolved (she may be an additional daughter). Styled ‘Captain’ (militia title; the Revolutionary War captaincy on the 1966 chart is Lead, not verified against a unit). Document Title: Benjamin T. Moore — CANDIDATE enslaver (NOT proven): b. NC 1813, lawyer, nephew of Gov. Gabriel Moore, court clerk, pardoned 1866; 1860 slave schedule read from the manuscript — ~95–96 people, NW Div, stamped pp. 487–488
Source: NARA M653, Roll 30, 1860 U.S. census slave schedule, Madison County AL, North Western Division, handwritten pp. 14–15 (stamped 487–488), read directly from the microfilm scan 2026-09-27 (Internet Archive item populationschedu030unit). Biography: NCpedia (Gabriel Moore); Shapiro, "The Pardons of Madison County"; Boyd v. Scott, 52 U.S. 292; 1859–60 Huntsville Directory. Memo: ~/workspace/research_notes/turner-moore-plantation-20260927/memo.md. Documents in Drive: Beyond Avalon > "Moore Plantation Research - 2026-09-27" (folder id 1FbVUYTC8fgwQEhqy7v9FN9t_Ev_nLEyG).
Evidence: Benjamin T. Moore, born North Carolina 1813, lawyer, nephew of Gov. Gabriel Moore; clerk of the U.S. District Court at Huntsville (by 1850/51 through 1859–60), then clerk of the Confederate district court (Northern District of AL); pardoned 1866 under the 1st and 13th exceptions. He took over most of Gabriel Moore's Madison County property in the 1830s while Gabriel was in Washington (the "swindle" transfers), followed by chancery litigation (Moore et al. v. Moore, 17 Ala. 628 (1850)). The 1860 slave schedule entry: "Benj. T. Moore," enumerated June 12–13, 1860, running from right-column line 22 of p. 14 through all of p. 15 — 19 adult men on p. 14 (ages 60, 43, 40, 30×4, 28×3, 27, 26, 25, 20×5), 77 people on p. 15 (30 male, 47 female per the page foot), total ~95–96, with a 60-year-old Black male heading the entry — Turner Moore's age cohort (b. ~1800–1810). Slave schedules do not name individuals: Turner's presence is UNPROVEN. Shapiro's pardon-list figure of "39 slaves" is DISPROVEN by this manuscript read — do not cite it.
Why It Is Important: The first named candidate enslaver with a manuscript-verified holding: a 95-person plantation in the Northwestern Division, assembled from a governor's estate, in Turner Moore's lifetime. Everything is sourced; the single missing piece is Turner himself in the entry.
Connections: DB1 1810 (Gabriel Moore); DB1 1817 (Alexander P. Jones adjacency); DB2 137 (Turner Moore); DB1 1718–1719 (Rathbun anchor).
Conclusions: Benjamin T. Moore is the named candidate; the manuscript holding is verified; Turner's presence is not.
