Document Title: Enoch Ensley, Sr. — Davidson County wealth, church deed, and death
Source: Haywood et al. v. Ensley & Haywood, 27 Tenn. 460 (1847); Williams v. Williams (Tenn. Dec. Term 1873), via static.case.law; Tusculum Cumberland Presbyterian Church history (cumberland.org); Nashville History blog (Davidson County court records)
Evidence: Described in 1847 as 'a neighbor, living on the adjoining tract of land, who was a man of wealth, and could at all times command any amount of money he might desire.' Purchased the 211 acres at the 1835 chancery sale (confirmed November 12, 1835); the 1847 decree made him trustee for Susan C. Haywood and her children. 1836: appointed to take Davidson County taxable property lists in Captain James Rains' company. 1835–36: commissioner for the Nashville–Nolensville turnpike. November 21, 1851: deeded the Tusculum meeting-house lot on the Nolensville Turnpike for the Cumberland Presbyterian Church (the history confirms the Tusculum name came from Judge Haywood's home 'to the north of the church property'). Died 1866 in Davidson County; will probated there; devised $50,000 in property to grandson Melville Williams; only son Enoch Ensley, Jr. was residuary legatee.
Why It Is Important: Identifies the 211-acre purchaser as a major Davidson County figure whose estate papers may show what became of the tract after 1847. The 1851 church deed independently anchors the Tusculum place-name to Judge Haywood's home.
Connections: Judge John Haywood; Tusculum; Susan C. Haywood.
Conclusions: Ensley's identity and wealth are established; the post-1847 disposition of the 211 acres is unknown.
Questions: Davidson County deed books after 1847; Ensley's 1866 estate file.
Citation: https://static.case.law/tenn/62/case-pdfs/0055-01.pdf

Document Title: Spotswood Jones contradiction RESOLVED — obituary's 'Mr. Spotswood Jones' = John Nelson Spotswood Jones
Source: 1876 Athens Post 'In Memoriam' obituary (May-scan Donnella); Jan 14, 1841 deed of gift; Encyclopedia of Alabama Donnell House article; Donnell genealogy site (Cumberland Presbyterian Church Donnell Family Information); Thomas Hubbard Hobbs journal Sept 28, 1852 (via 'King Cotton to Space Capital,' yumpu)
Evidence: The obituary calls Maria L. Jones 'daughter of Mr. Spotswood Jones, of Limestone county, Ala.' Four converging points identify him as John Nelson Spotswood Jones: (1) the Jan 14, 1841 deed has J.N.S. Jones granting ten enslaved people 'to daughter Maria Louisa Donnell'; (2) EOA's Donnell House article names Maria's father-in-law as 'John Nelson Spotswood Jones'; (3) the Donnell genealogy compilation lists Maria as 'daughter of John Nelson Spottswood Jones and Eliza Haywood'; (4) Limestone County diarist Thomas Hubbard Hobbs, writing Sept 28, 1852, calls Eliza 'Mrs. Spotswood Jones' — contemporary local usage of 'Spotswood Jones' for J.N.S. No independent 'Spotswood Jones of Limestone County' appears in any record searched.
Why It Is Important: Closes the DB4 contradiction (row 1039); confirms Maria Louisa Jones Donnell's parentage as J.N.S. Jones's daughter; documents the family's local naming practice.
Connections: Maria Louisa Jones Donnell; John Nelson Spotswood Jones; Eliza Haywood Jones; 1841 deed of gift (Sept item 27); DB4 row 1039
Conclusions: The obituary's 'Mr. Spotswood Jones' is a garbled/abbreviated reference to John Nelson Spotswood Jones — not a separate person. No merge was ever needed; no second person exists.

Document Title: James Jones's Jamaican factoring network — Simon Taylor, John Tailyour, the King George and the Hester (Radburn, WMQ 2015)
Source: Nicholas Radburn, 'Guinea Factors, Slave Sales and the Profits of the trans-Atlantic Slave Trade in Late Eighteenth-Century Jamaica: The Case of John Tailyour,' William and Mary Quarterly 3rd Ser., 72, 2 (April 2015); free full text https://eprints.lancs.ac.uk/id/eprint/88417/1/Radburn_WMQ_Apr_2015.pdf
Evidence: September 1787: Simon Taylor — 'one of the richest sugar planters in the British Atlantic' (Radburn) — wrote to James Jones, 'by then Bristol's principal slave trading merchant,' advertising the creditworthiness of his cousin John Tailyour's new Kingston factoring company. Three months later Jones sent his ship King George to Tailyour. 19 December 1789: Jones's ship Hester arrived Kingston with 299 African captives, consigned to Tailyour's factoring house; the sale opened about three weeks later and Simon Taylor bought eight 'prime' men and one woman for his Golden Grove plantation, naming three of them Taylor, Simon, and John. Sustained correspondence, Tailyour to James Jones at Kingston: 30 May 1788; 15 Feb 1789; 31 May 1789; 22 Nov 1789; 26 Dec 1789; 24 Jan 1790; 25 Jul 1791; 15 Jan 1792.
Why It Is Important: First documented evidence of James Jones's direct business relationship with the Jamaican planter elite — Simon Taylor, the richest sugar planter in the British Atlantic, dealt with Jones personally and bought the Hester's captives for Golden Grove. Upgrades the paper's [402] 'Tailyour's letter' shorthand to a full 1787–1792 commercial relationship. The archival source family behind the article (Tailyour Family Papers, William L. Clements Library, Univ. of Michigan; Taylor/Vanneck-Arcedekne Papers, Commonwealth Institute London) is the strongest new lead for the conversion-mechanism question — the letterbooks document the bills of exchange and sugar consignments that carried slaving profits back to Bristol.
Connections: DB1 rows 1429–1448 (James Jones will, PROB 11/1259/104); DB1 row 1491 (62-voyage fleet quantified, with the 2026-09-28 correction that no record connects Bristol wealth to the Madison County Joneses); DB1 row 1522 (Richardson/Stone historiography); paper [402]/[705].
Conclusions: Verified as stated. James Jones of Bristol did direct, sustained business with Simon Taylor and John Tailyour, 1787–1792 — the Hester's 299 captives and the King George consignment are documented in the Tailyour papers. This is a fact about James Jones of Bristol; it does NOT connect his wealth to the Madison County Joneses — the Bristol-to-Madison conversion remains Unresolved.

Document Title: Morgan BRS vol. 80 (2025) — verified Jones voyage data (James Jones, Bristol)
Document Type: Published primary-source edition (transcribed documents + editorial notes)
Source: UK sweep 2; Kenneth Morgan (ed.), Documents on the Bristol Slave Trade, BRS vol. 80 (2025), Internet Archive bristol-record-society-80
Evidence: Full-text search (106 'Jones' hits) verified: (1) James Jones managed 68 slave voyages from Bristol 1783-1795 (Richardson, The Bristol Slave Traders, p. 29) — UPDATES the 62-voyage figure. (2) Thomas Jones managed 34 slave voyages 1767-1794 (same, p. 29) — the major Bristol trader; firewall stands (not James's brother Thomas). (3) Royal Charlotte: Joseph Jackson master; owners James Jones, Thomas Deane, Richard Stratton, Thomas Rigge; left Bristol 5 May 1787; 455 embarked Bonny; 417 disembarked Grenada; returned 14 Feb 1788; voyage ID 18005. (4) King George: Alexander Robe master, James Jones owner; left Bristol 31 May 1787; 453 embarked Bonny; 415 disembarked Kingston; returned 12 Apr 1788; ID 17998 — matches Radburn (sent to Tailyour at Kingston). (5) Hester: William Jenkins/John Langley masters, James Jones owner; left Bristol 29 Feb 1788; 320/400 embarked Anomabu/Cape Coast Castle; 299 disembarked Jamaica; ended Boston 24 Mar 1790; ID 18018 — 299 matches Radburn's 19 Dec 1789 Kingston arrival. (6) Brothers: Jeffrey Howlett master, James Jones owner; left Bristol 6 July 1787; 450 embarked Gold Coast; 412 disembarked Grenada; returned 12 Feb 1789; ID 17985. (7) James: left Bristol 3 Sept 1787; 169 embarked Windward Coast; 154 disembarked Black River, Jamaica; returned 2 May 1789; ID 17996. (8) Lovely Lass: John Kennedy/William Jenkins masters; left Bristol 27 May 1788; 408 embarked Gold Coast; 398 disembarked Jamaica; returned 25 Aug 1789; ID 18025. (9) Mary, 19 Feb 1791: Thomas Jones AND James Jones co-owners; Edward Mentor master; 165 embarked New Calabar; 158 disembarked Grenada; returned 21 Oct 1791; ID 18108 — commercial link between the two Joneses, NOT an identity merge. (10) Wasp, 13 Nov 1787: Thomas Jones owner; 248 embarked New Calabar; 230 disembarked Kingston; ID 18012. (11) Eliza, 4 Mar 1789: Thomas Jones, Charles Harford, Thomas Rigge owners; 283 embarked; 210 disembarked St. Vincent/Jamaica; ID 18041.
Why It Is Important: Gives citable voyage-level data for James Jones's fleet; the 68-voyage figure supersedes 62; the Mary co-ownership documents a Jones-Jones commercial link without merging identities; voyage IDs are now citable via Richardson/Bristol vol. 4.
Conclusions: Verified fleet data; co-ownership is commercial, not identity.

Document Title: Jones letter 7 Nov 1793 — bills of exchange for slave cargoes (capital mechanism)
Source: UK sweep 2; Morgan (ed.), Documents on the Bristol Slave Trade, BRS vol. 80 (2025), document reproducing: 'Jones, Bristol, to John Taylor, London, 7 November 1793, Tailyour Papers'
Evidence: James Jones writes: 'I received the account sales & bills for the Royal Charlotte's & Nassau's cargoes. Why It Is Important: First document in hand showing HOW the Bristol wealth moved as financial instruments — the mechanism behind the conversion question.
Connections: DB1 2382 (Tailyour Papers), 1058-1059 (money-trail questions)

Source: Bedford County chancery, LVA 1823-012, image-only PDF

Document Title: Mark Anthony v Daniel Jones & Edward Jones — bill of injunction over a £130 Bedford land bond, plus 1810 amendment alleging the assignment to Edward Jones was fictitious
Document Type: Chancery manuscript — firsthand read of all page images (33/33)
Source: Library of Virginia, Bedford County chancery causes, 1826-016
Evidence: Bill sworn at Bedford June Court 1807 (J. Steptoe C.C.): sometime in 1804 Mark Anthony bought a tract of land in Bedford County from Daniel Jones for £200 — express term that no money was to be paid, price to be discharged entirely in bonds and horses. Anthony paid £70 (the first payment) in "a horse and watch," and gave his own bond for the £130 residue, conditioned to be discharged within twelve months by other bonds to £100 plus a horse valued at £30. Before the year expired Anthony delivered Jones a horse at £33 (credited) and offered Jones several bonds in part discharge, telling Jones he would be ready to fulfil the bond's condition; Jones replied Anthony "need not be particular about discharging the condition of his obligation before the time mentioned in your Orators Bond" but asked interest from the bond's due date, promising the condition would not be forfeited and that he would thereafter take other bonds in lieu. Relying on this, Anthony let the time elapse; Jones then, "without ever mentioning the subject to your Orator, assigned the aforesaid bond to one Edward Jones," who sued at law and obtained a judgment. Anthony prays injunction. Amendment sworn before John Steptoe 23 July 1810: Anthony now believes the Daniel-to-Edward assignment "was merely fictitious," that Edward "was only intended as a Trustee for the said Daniel," and that under this impression Anthony has paid Daniel the full amount — prays relief if the assignment was fictitious.
Why It Is Important: The founding document of a 22-year injunction suit (1807–1829); names Daniel Jones selling Bedford land in 1804 on bonds-and-horses terms; the fictitious-assignment allegation (trustee relationship between Daniel and Edward Jones) is pleaded but never adjudicated in the file.

Document Title: Heritage Book: Edmund Townsend — ~300 enslaved people, 1833 will, broken by heirs
Source: Madison County Heritage Book (1998), 'The Jones Homeplace' entry, book p. 78. Submitted by Amber Maria Jones, Hazel Green, AL.
Evidence: Edmund Townsend (b. 1791, Lunenburg County, Va.) moved to Madison County 1819; bought over 6,000 acres. At his death (April 12, 1833), 'the plantation, land, personal property, tools, stock, and approximately 300 slaves, were appraised for $88,000.' His will (January 25, 1833) 'bequeathed $10,000 to his slave-sons, Armstead and Woodson. He left his slave-daughters, "Eliza M. and Virginia Townsend, all his land, stock, tools, furniture, negroes, all 'money' due him. The executors were to 'petition the Legislature of the state to grant them [his children] their freedom and to be allowed to remain in the state.' Edmund's relatives filed suit stating slave-children were property. "Property" could not own property. Years of legal arguments followed. The Court ruled all property should be sold including the children. Relatives broke the will, inherited the money and purchased the land, slaves and personal property.'
Why It Is Important: MAJOR people/capital finding. Edmund Townsend held ~300 enslaved people on a 6,000-acre Madison County plantation ($88,000 appraisal, 1833). His will attempted to free and provide for his enslaved children (Armstead, Woodson, Eliza M., Virginia Townsend); white relatives broke the will and the court ordered the children sold as property. The Townsend family are the Jones-network neighbors the user flagged. Names Armstead, Woodson, Eliza M., and Virginia Townsend go to DB2 as enslaved people. The will contest is a paper-level story about capital, kinship, and the law.

Document Title: Jones v. Perkins — the two legal holdings (better title in stranger; co-tenant ouster rule)
Source: 1 Stew. 512, headnotes 1-2
Evidence: Holding 1: In trespass to try titles, a defendant in possession under claim of right (not a mere trespasser) may defeat the plaintiff by proving better title in a stranger. The 'no adverse title in a stranger' rule applies only to a mere trespasser without color of title; APJ 'was the heir at law to one third of the premises in dispute, as a tenant in the nature of a coparcener with his brother and sister, and could in no wise be viewed as a mere intruder.' Holding 2: 'One tenant in common cannot maintain the action of trespass to try titles against a co-tenant, without proving an actual ouster.'
Why It Is Important: The holdings matter for the family story: even if Richard had validly acquired Benjamin's third, he would have been only a tenant in common with APJ and could not recover without proving ouster. The law protected the heir in possession.
Connections: Alexander P. Jones; tenancy in common; trespass to try titles
Conclusions: Two holdings, both favoring the heir in possession.

Document Title: Jones v. Perkins, 1 Stewart 512-514 (Ala. Supreme Court) — full opinion text
Source: Free Law Project / CourtListener static scan (public domain, 1830)
Evidence: Caption: 'Jones v. Perkins.' Richard Perkins brought trespass to try title in Madison County Circuit Court against Alexander P. Jones for an undivided third of a tract, claiming under a deed from Benjamin Perkins, who claimed a life estate as husband of, and in right of, his wife — 'a daughter of Lewellen Jones, and entitled to one third of his estate.' The court states: 'the premises sued for are a part of the estate of Lewellen Jones, deceased; that the said deceased left two sons, Alexander P. [Jones] the defendant below, John N. S. Jones, and Mrs Perkins, the wife of Benjamin Perkins, his heirs at law.' Alexander offered to prove Benjamin Perkins's title had vested by sheriff's sale in Thomas Moore, a judgment creditor of Benjamin, prior to the sale to Richard Perkins — rejected below. Held: reversed and remanded; the defendant, as heir at law (tenant in the nature of a coparcener, not a mere trespasser), could defeat the plaintiff by proving paramount title in a stranger; one tenant in common cannot maintain trespass to try titles against a co-tenant without proving actual ouster. Counsel: Clay and McClung for the plaintiff in error; Kelly and Hutchinson for the defendant. Judge Saffold not sitting; opinion by the Chief Justice.
Why It Is Important: Establishes Lewellen Jones's three heirs at law from a primary court source: Alexander P. Jones, John N. S. Jones, and Mrs. Perkins (wife of Benjamin Perkins), each entitled to one third of the estate. Confirms Benjamin Perkins married Lewellen's daughter (Frances Ann/Anna Maria). Documents a sheriff's-sale transfer of Benjamin Perkins's interest to Thomas Moore (judgment creditor) — a capital-depletion signal.
Connections: DB4 rows 111 (Frances identity), 112 (case text), 94 (J.N.S. Jones identity); Lewellen Jones 1818 will (Madison Co., April Term 1820, p. 106); 1805 deed of gift (Frances Ann Maria Jones); 1824 Benjamin Perkins to Richard Perkins deed (Book D, p. 706, 'Int. in Est. of L. Jones').
Conclusions: Lewellen Jones died leaving three heirs at law: sons Alexander P. Jones and John N. S. Jones, and daughter Mrs. Perkins (wife of Benjamin Perkins). The case does NOT mention the 1820 manumission of Elizabeth or any enslaved person — it is a land-title dispute among the heirs; the timeline's characterization of it as a manumission-title case should be corrected.
Questions: Did Thomas Moore (judgment creditor) retain the one-third interest, or did it revert? What tract was the 'certain tract of land in said county'?

Document Title: Jones v. Fort (36 Ala. 449, 1860) — trover for the hired slave Orange
Source: Alabama Reports vol. 36 (June Term 1860), Harvard Library Innovation Lab scan via static.case.law
Evidence: Firsthand read of the opinion (Harvard Library Innovation Lab PDF via static.case.law): Rachel M. Jones (Dallas County) sued Elias W. Fort and Gabriel H. Fort in trover for the loss of an enslaved man named Orange. She had hired Orange to her son-in-law Squire Lowry for 1858; on Dec 24, 1858 Lowry's sons loaned Orange to the Forts to help raise a gin-house about a half-mile from Lowry's plantation (itself ~16 miles from Marion); a timber fell and killed him. Held: a hirer's gratuitous loan of a hired slave to another for gin-house raising makes the sub-bailee liable to the owner in trover for the slave's value, no matter what care was exercised. CAUTION: the volume's errata flags the 6th and 8th headnotes as erroneous (corrected in the index, pp. 744–745, tit. Bailment) — cite the opinion text, not the headnotes.
Why It Is Important: Citable Alabama hiring-out/sub-bailment doctrine: a gratuitous sub-loan of a hired enslaved person triggers trover liability for the owner regardless of the care exercised. Documents the named enslaved man Orange and the exact 1858 Dallas County chain — the clearest published Alabama parallel to APJ-era hiring-out practices.
Connections: Hiring-out case-law; ties to DB4 rows 374 (resolved), 369 (labor-force management). Rachel M. Jones is Dallas County only — do-not-merge with Madison/Avalon Joneses.
Questions: Whether the Forts were kin to any Madison County Jones/Perkins/Anderson line (not yet checked).

Document Title: Bedford chancery 019-1820-022: enslaved watermen WILL (head man), JAMES & JACK, owned by Richard Perkins, hired to William L. Adams, 1803
Source: Bedford Co. chancery cause 019-1820-022 (Library of Virginia digitized chancery collection, pulled from Mac Session-Archives 8.9.26)
Evidence: Richard Murray's affidavit (taken at the house of Jesse Moore, Albemarle, 19 Feb 1806, image 0023): 'do you not believe the the three watermen Will, James, & Jack were the only watermen that Richard Perkins owned in the year 1803? Answer — I am very sure he had none other, and I believe they were hired to Wm L. Adams.' Murray: 'the work was done by the above named Watermen in the year 1803. about the 20th of March and I paid the freight to Richard Perkins' (about 70 bushels wheat at 9d/bushel); also ~30 bushels of Richard Perkins's, 5–6 bushels of John Perkins's, and two hogsheads of tobacco of Richard & John Perkins's were carried in the same boat. Jesse Moore's affidavit (19 Feb 1806, image 0025): 'on the first day of February 1803 A certain Negroe waterman Named Will — belonging to Richard Perkins of Fluvanna — applyd to him for loading to load a boat — which this affiant furnished the sd Negroe with and continued to furnish several loads afterwards having furnished the last on the 11th day of March following amounting in all to one hundred & Forty six barrels of flour at Two Shillings & six pence per barrel freight all of which freight money this affiant gave the said Negroe An order on the Merchants of Richmond for.' Will told Moore 'he was hired to Mr. Adams.' Plaintiff's question: 'did the said Waterman Will bring with him any written order from William L Adams authorising him to engage loading for the Benefit of said Adams. Answer — he did not.' Moore: 'do you not believe that the said Will and his hands were the negroes which were hired to me by Richard Perkins. Answer — I do.' Jesse Moore's second affidavit (15 Sept 1806, image 0031): 'Three Negroe men (known to this Affiant to be the property of [Richard Perkins] the defendant) Applyed to him for loading for a Batteaux' — they were 'then working in the service of said Adams'; he furnished 146 barrels of flour at 2s6d/barrel freight over the winter; on return they produced receipts for delivery in Richmond; defendant Perkins's question calls Will 'the head man of the boat.' Richard Hall's affidavit (3 Aug 1805, image 0009): Adams 'informed the negroes that he had hired them, and gave them orders what to do, particularly to go down the river after a boat, and to procure work where they could find it.' Sandy D. Duncan's affidavit (3 Aug 1805, image 0010): Adams 'gave orders to the head man' to take the boat down the river after the holidays. Thomas Tillman's receipts for Walter Irvine & Co (images 0046, 0048): 'Will has delivered a Receipt to us for carriage of 155-50th Bushels Wheat @ 9d — £5.16.9. Carriage 3 hhds Tob 4315 — 1/ — 2.3.1 — £8.19.10. 26th Jany 1803 for W Irvin & Co'; 'Will has delivered us a receipt for the delivery of Two hhds Tobacco in Richmond... N Canton 23d Mar 1803 for Walter Irvine & Co.'
Why It Is Important: Three NAMED enslaved men — WILL (the head man/boat captain), JAMES, JACK — owned by Richard Perkins of Fluvanna and hired out to William L. Adams for 1803. Will is documented as a skilled river waterman: he negotiated loading (146 barrels of flour from Jesse Moore, 2s6d/barrel freight = £18.5.0), delivered receipts to Richmond merchants, and worked a batteau on the upper James. This is a rare named-individual window into the enslaved James River freight economy, with itemized wages-in-kind, distances (Richmond to Warminster/Warren), and the 'head man' hierarchy among hired watermen. PEOPLE thread at its most concrete.
Connections: Will (enslaved waterman, head man); James (enslaved waterman); Jack (enslaved waterman); Richard Perkins (owner, Fluvanna); William L. Adams (hirer); Jesse Moore (Albemarle, flour shipper); Richard Murray; Richard Hall; Sandy D. Duncan; Walter Irvine & Co; Thomas Tillman; Rives Higginbotham & Co.
Conclusions: Will, James, and Jack are the first Perkins-enslaved people with documented names, occupations, and labor history. Will's role as head man of the boat (seeking loads, handling Richmond merchants, carrying receipts) shows skilled enslaved river labor with real agency within the freight system.

Conclusions: The Huntsville claims agent acted as advocate as well as processor, pushing back on evidentiary rules that disadvantaged Black widows.
Questions: Did Elvira Gordon receive the bounty? What was Howard's ruling on remarriage and on illiterate witnesses?

Document Title: Geography of bounty payment — Wager argues against moving the pay station to Florence; merchants, 'charitable' intermediaries, and the Freedmen's Bank contest freedpeople's money (Mar 1870)
Source: IA recordsoffieldof0016unit (NARA M1900 reel 16), pp. 88-89
Evidence: Letters Sent Vol 3 (68), book pp. 74-79: John W. Wager to Maj Gen O.O. Howard, March 29 1870, answering Howard's March 26 letter proposing a move to Florence (Lauderdale Co.). Wager argues: (1) few late colored soldiers in Lauderdale Co.; most live in counties south of the Tennessee River west of Decatur, for whom Florence is as costly as Huntsville; (2) checks cannot be cashed at Tuscumbia/Courtland/Florence — former Tuscumbia agent J.M. Green had to carry checks to Memphis, claimants paying expenses; (3) fare Florence-Huntsville $4.35 per person; claimant + two witnesses × 6 trips = $26.10, plus $8.70 for the payment trip; (4) local merchants have credited soldiers against expected bounties and fear soldiers will spend the money before reaching home; (5) merchants dislike Wager urging soldiers to deposit in the Freedmen's Bank, and spread the claim that deposits are compelled; (6) 'charitable persons' like 'Mr Jones' write offering to 'help the colored men and save their money,' but 'it generally turns out they have an axe of their own to grind' — Wager does not know Mr Jones personally; (7) 'Mr W M Reese' stands well with Republicans and colored men and Wager would recommend him as agent, though it would be unfair to others; (8) many claims in Morgan, Lawrence, Colbert counties remain unpaid, and many never applied (some via W.M. Baker) for lack of travel money.
Why It Is Important: A panoramic CAPITAL-thread document: every party in the district — merchants, bank agents, 'charitable' letter-writers, rival attorneys — is positioning to intercept Black soldiers' federal bounty money, and the claims agent is defending his Huntsville pay station as the least-bad option. Quantifies the travel-cost barrier ($34.80 total) that kept poor claimants from filing at all. Also documents Freedmen's Bank deposit promotion and the backlash it drew.
Connections: J.M. Green (former Tuscumbia agent, DB2 staged); W.M. Baker (Courtland attorney); Freedmen's Bank; DB1-3638 (Wilson fraud); 'Mr Jones' (DB4 question).
Conclusions: The bounty system imposed steep transaction costs (travel, witnesses, uncashable checks) that functioned as a filter; local white economic actors (merchants extending credit against bounties) had a direct interest in where and how the money was paid.
Questions: Who was 'Mr Jones'? Who was W.M. Reese? Did the Department move the station? How many Morgan/Lawrence/Colbert claims were ever paid?

Conclusions: The claims agent doubled as a violence reporter; the Bureau's paper trail captures Reconstruction terror that never made it into the claims ledgers.
